content: This review focuses on interventions for drug-using offenders who also have co-occurring mental health problems, aiming to determine the most effective treatments for reducing drug use and criminal activity in this population. The review included 13 studies with a total of 2,606 participants, and interventions were delivered in various settings, including prisons, courts, community settings, and medium-secure hospitals. 1. Therapeutic Community Interventions: Four studies evaluated therapeutic community interventions. Compared to treatment as usual (two studies, 266 participants), therapeutic community interventions moderately reduced the likelihood of subsequent criminal activity (risk ratio [RR] 0.67, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.53 to 0.84) and return to prison (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.67). Compared to cognitive-behavioral therapy (one study, 314 participants), there was no significant reduction in self-reported drug use (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.32), re-arrest for any crime (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.09), criminal activity (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.05), or drug-related crime (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.36). This evidence was of low certainty. Compared to a waiting list control (one study, 478 participants), therapeutic community interventions significantly reduced the likelihood of returning to prison (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.79), with moderate-certainty evidence. 2. Mental Health Treatment Courts: One study (235 participants) compared a mental health treatment court with an assertive case management model to treatment as usual. At 12 months, there was no significant reduction in self-reported drug use on the Addiction Severity Index (mean difference [MD] 0.00, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.03), conviction for a new crime (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.22), or re-incarceration (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.01). This evidence was of low certainty. 3. Motivational Interviewing and Mindfulness-Based Interventions: Four studies compared motivational interviewing or mindfulness-based interventions to relaxation therapy, a waiting list control, or treatment as usual. Compared to relaxation therapy (one study), participants in the motivational interviewing group reported fewer marijuana-related problems at three months, with moderate-certainty evidence. Compared to a waiting list control (one study, 31 participants), there was no significant reduction in self-reported drug use (MD -0.04, 95% CI -0.37 to 0.29) or abstinence from drug use (RR 2.89, 95% CI 0.73 to 11.43) at six months. This evidence was of low certainty. Compared to treatment as usual (two studies, 40 participants), there was no significant reduction in marijuana use frequency at three months post-release (MD -1.05, 95% CI -2.39 to 0.29) or time to first arrest (MD 0.87, 95% CI -0.12 to 1.86). However, there was a small reduction in re-arrest frequency (MD -0.66, 95% CI -1.31 to -0.01) up to 36 months. Another study (80 participants) found no significant reduction in positive drug screens at 12 months (MD -0.7, 95% CI -3.5 to 2.1), with very low-certainty evidence. 4. Multi-Systemic Therapy: Two studies evaluated multi-systemic therapy involving juveniles and families. Compared to treatment as usual (156 participants), there was no significant reduction in drug dependence (MD -0.22, 95% CI -2.51 to 2.07) or arrests (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.36) up to seven months. This evidence was of low certainty. Compared to adolescent substance abuse therapy (112 participants), there was a significant reduction in re-arrests up to 24 months (MD 0.24, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.28), based on low-certainty evidence. 5. Interpersonal Psychotherapy: One study (38 participants) compared interpersonal psychotherapy to a psychoeducational intervention. There was no significant reduction in self-reported drug use at three months (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.50), with very low-certainty evidence. 6. Legal Defense and Wrap-Around Services: One study (29 participants) compared legal defense services combined with wrap-around social work services to legal defense services alone. There was no significant reduction in the number of new offenses committed at 12 months (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.07 to 6.01), with very low-certainty evidence. Conclusions: Therapeutic community interventions and mental health treatment courts may reduce subsequent drug use and criminal activity among drug-using offenders with co-occurring mental health problems. However, the evidence for other interventions, such as interpersonal psychotherapy, multi-systemic therapy, legal defense wrap-around services, and motivational interviewing, is less certain. The variability in study designs and outcomes necessitates caution when interpreting the results.
